title: Does the top bid get the top ad?
hook: Ad A bids more per click than ad B. Is A sure to get the top slot?

knows: ads can be sold by auction
doesNotKnow: that when ads are ranked by bid times a quality score, a lower bid can win the top slot and pay less

misconception: The highest bidder always gets the top ad slot.
objective: The learner can rank two ads by bid × quality, see that the lower bid can come first, and work out that under a pay-the-least-that-keeps-your-rank rule the winner pays the next ad's score divided by its own quality.

claims.text: Ranked by bid alone, A's $2.00 beats B's $1.50 and takes the top slot.
Ranked by bid × quality, B scores $1.50 × 1.0 = 1.5 and A scores $2.00 × 0.5 = 1.0, so B takes the top slot with the lower bid.
claims.source: Arithmetic; Demo.tsx key(…, 'score'). Brief check in company/domains/briefs/economics.markets.md #22.

claims.text: Under the rule 'pay the least bid that keeps your slot', B pays 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = $1.00 a click, less than A bid.
claims.source: B stays on top for any bid above A's score ÷ B's quality = 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = $1.00 (equal at $1.00); price = next score ÷ own quality. Demo.tsx B_PRICE.

claims.text: With B's bid at $0.80, B's score 0.8 falls below A's 1.0 and A takes the top slot (and pays 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = $1.60 a click); at $1.00 the two tie.
The ranking and payment rule are a simplified model with invented numbers, not a description of any real search engine.
claims.source: Stage chip states the payment rule; reveal footnote. The brief's planned claim about real search engines (quality factor used, formulas not public; E&K ch. 15) needs a human source check and is kept out of learner text.

recall.question: Ads are ranked by bid × quality. Ad P bids $3 with quality 0.4; ad Q bids $2 with quality 0.8. Which ad is ranked first?
recall.why: P scores 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 and Q scores 2 × 0.8 = 1.6. The product decides, so the lower bid can win.
